content:
Hi all,

This month I have fully transcribed a famous handwritten working notes corpus from Grothendieck Montpellier archives, I took it from a handwritten text recognition challenge at first (it is known to be a very chaotic corpus), but then continued with AI-assisted data analysis and LEAN formalization.

I found five important conjectures during the process and also some unpublished proofs that were easy to verify with my machine.

Do you think it can be interesting to formalize these five conjectures in the formal-conjectures repo ? A math expert would of course need to state if the conjectures make sense, but it's more or less what Grothendieck has written. I have also contacted a few researchers directly, without an answer so far, so I am asking here as well.

The one for the homotopy hypothesis was mentioned in the working notes, and claimed recently by OpenAI end of September. "The Grothendieck homotopy hypothesis via elementary expansions", and conjecture had been explained by Maltsiniotis in this talk. And 2 others have been claimed by OpenAI in the list.

Writing the conjectures explicitly also show that OpenAI only covered special cases of the 3 claimed conjectures.

Some of you also have seen some PRs I did in the mathlib4 repo for more basic results from the notes.

Tell me what you think about it especially if you think this is too "aggressive" approach.

One risk of taking conjectures from unrefereed notes is that they might be obviously wrong for stupid reasons but hiding a good idea, and may need to be adjusted (eg by restricting to special cases). Not saying that's happened here, but note that the source of problems in the Erdos problems site is not "anything Erdos ever asked to anyone" but "anything which went through a referee process".

Thank you. I was also thinking about applying the same procedure (transcription / modernization / formalization) for older manuscripts or typescripts which are available online:

  • French mathematicians online archive at French National library BnF
  • Bourbaki archives

17th to mid 20th century maths having been mostly written by French and British scientists. Obviously speaking French helps. Because they are classics, these notes, theorems or conjectures have been reviewed in other books or articles already, and just need some literature research which AI assitants can also do (even for the 5 conjectures from Grothendieck above).

Kevin Buzzard said:

One risk of taking conjectures from unrefereed notes is that they might be obviously wrong for stupid reasons but hiding a good idea, and may need to be adjusted (eg by restricting to special cases). Not saying that's happened here, but note that the source of problems in the Erdos problems site is not "anything Erdos ever asked to anyone" but "anything which went through a referee process".

Absolutely agree! One way of dealing with that would be to ask on Mathoverflow. In the past, we have merged PRs with statements of questions from MO that seem interesting but hadn't received a full answer.

Ok it feels like I will have to abandon this then, and continue discussion on Mathoverflow.

Thank you for your honest comments.

Please note the 3 proofs from OpenAI I mentioned above have no formalization in the formal-conjectures repo.

Here are the modern sources :

  • Standard conjectures: Grothendieck, Standard conjectures on algebraic cycles, Bombay 1969.
  • Generalised Hodge: Grothendieck, Hodge’s general conjecture is false for trivial reasons, Topology 1969.
  • p-curvature: Katz, 1970 and 1972.
  • Homotopy hypothesis: Pursuing Stacks, now published by the SMF (Documents mathématiques).
  • Section conjecture and Galois action on Teichmüller towers: the Letter to Faltings and the Esquisse, published in Schneps–Lochak (LMS Lecture Notes 242, 1997).

Just to be clear, I think we should absolutely formalise such problems. I think the point that Kevin was making is that for less well known problems (e.g. problems that are only ever mentioned in unrefereed notes - which isn't the case for the problems you have in mind:)), it's worth checking with experts in the field to make sure that these are problems that are worth spending time on.

If you do decide to work on formalising these, I think a good place to get started could be contributing the necessary prerequisites to TauCeti! Many of these prerequisites (definitions, etc) for these conjectures would be of general interest for other people in these areas who are interested in formalisation
Note also that there is already work in progress on formalising some of these (e.g. the Hodge conjecture)

"worth checking with experts in the field to make sure that these are problems that are worth spending time on"
OpenAI tried to solve three of them for particular cases.

Thank you I just did a couple of pull requests to TauCetiRoadmap
